livy_content: caritas annonae then fames after the secession left fields untilled
machiavelli_content: essendo Roma, come avviene, venuta in penuria grande di vettovaglie
notes: Event retained; but 'come avviene' (as happens) normalizes a specific post-secession shock into a recurrent condition.

livy_content: cause given: fields untilled during the plebeian secession (ex incultis per secessionem plebis agris)
notes: The politically significant supply-side cause (the plebs' own strike caused the shortage Coriolanus then weaponized) is dropped; the famine becomes exogenous.

livy_content: purchasing agents sent along three routes: Etruria via Ostia, Volscian coast to Cumae, and Sicily
machiavelli_content: avendo il Senato mandato per grani in Sicilia
notes: Three-route logistics compressed to the single politically salient source (Sicily, whose arrival triggers the debate). Also an actor shift: Livy credits the consuls (ni consules providissent); Machiavelli credits the Senate.

livy_content: grain bought at Cumae; ships seized by the tyrant Aristodemus as heir to the Tarquins' property
notes: A striking sovereign-risk/diplomatic detail (dynastic claims interfering with food logistics) entirely dropped.

livy_content: ex Tuscis frumentum Tiberi venit; eo sustentata est plebs — Etruscan grain down the Tiber actually sustained the plebs
notes: The operative relief channel is omitted; in the Discorsi only the Sicilian (contested) grain exists.

livy_content: colonists added at Velitrae; new colony at Norba as a Pomptine stronghold
notes: Territorial-administrative response dropped (though colonies as safety valve appear in Disc I.37 for Case C).

livy_content: Senate debate is over the PRICE at which state grain should be sold (agitatum in senatu, quanti plebi daretur)
machiavelli_content: proposal framed as WITHHOLDING distribution outright: tenendola affamata, e non gli distribuendo il frumento
notes: Machiavelli converts a price-setting decision into a binary distribution decision, sharpening the episode into a starvation-leverage story. The administrative texture (pricing of public grain sales) is lost.

livy_content: Coriolanus's conditional bargain: old grain price only if the patres' old rights are restored (si annonam veterem volunt, ius pristinum reddant patribus)
machiavelli_content: consigliò come egli era venuto il tempo da potere gastigare la Plebe, e torle quella autorità
notes: Core political intent preserved accurately: grain leverage against the tribunate.

livy_content: named consuls (T. Geganius, P. Minucius; then M. Minucius, A. Sempronius), named tribune target (Sicinius)
machiavelli_content: anonymous institutions: il Senato, i Tribuni; only Coriolano named
notes: Systematic: individuals become offices. Only the exemplary protagonist keeps his name.

livy_content: in exeuntem e curia impetus factus esset, ni peropportune tribuni diem dixissent
machiavelli_content: allo uscire del Senato lo arebbero tumultuariamente morto, se gli Tribuni non lo avessero citato a comparire
notes: Near-verbatim preservation — the pivot of Machiavelli's argument, rendered faithfully.

livy_content: patricians deploy clients to deter individuals from meetings (dispositis clientibus absterrendo singulos a coitionibus conciliisque); then collective supplication
notes: Patronage as a counter-mobilization technology is dropped in I.7 — though the same mechanism (partisans via private favors) is theorized in Disc III.28. The omitted datum would have complicated the clean 'legal channel' story.

livy_content: condemned in absentia; exile among the Volsci; plotting war against Rome with Attius Tullius
notes: Machiavelli ends the story at the citation to trial. The sequel (exile → foreign war led by the condemned man) would cut against the lesson that the legal channel neutralized the danger: the channeled conflict still produced a Volscian war. Strategically bounded compression.

livy_content: Livy's micro-mechanism: rage subsided because each pleb saw himself become judge and master of his enemy's life (se iudicem quisque... factum videbat)
machiavelli_content: general law: le republiche con le leggi loro, diano onde sfogarsi all’ira che concepe la universalità contro a uno cittadino
notes: Livy's one-off crowd psychology is elevated into a standing institutional-design principle (the venting of umori through ordini). This is the central theoretical move of the chapter.

livy_content: Livy's authorial counterfactual: the patres could probably have traded grain-price relief for abolition of the tribunate
notes: Notable omission: Livy hands Machiavelli a ready-made counterfactual about buying back constitutional concessions with food policy, and Machiavelli — usually eager for such reasoning — drops it. It would undercut I.4's thesis that the tribunate was beneficial.

machiavelli_content: Francesco Valori's fall (Florence 1498): no ordinary channel to resist him; sects armed; Valori and other nobles killed
notes: Source: Machiavelli's direct contemporary knowledge (he entered the chancery weeks after Valori's death). Functions as the negative control case for the accusation-channel claim.

machiavelli_content: Piero Soderini's fall (1512): no accusation mode against powerful citizens; eight judges insufficient; opponents brought the Spanish army
notes: Source: direct professional experience — Machiavelli served under Soderini until the 1512 collapse. The 'otto giudici' is the Florentine Otto di Guardia: an administrative-institutional datum from his chancery world.

livy_content: — (episode is in Livy V.33, outside the aligned passage)
machiavelli_content: Arruns of Clusium invites the Gauls for lack of civic redress
notes: Other-source in the narrow sense: it is still Livy, but imported from Book V to serve the external-forces generalization. Machiavelli reshapes it: Livy V.33 gives wine-enticement and the wife of the guardian Lucumo; the 'sister of Arruns' is Machiavelli's (or his edition's) variant.

machiavelli_content: counterfactual: had Coriolanus been lynched, private offense → fear → defense → partisans → parties → ruin
notes: Explicit counterfactual chain with no Livian basis; the faction-cascade model is Machiavelli's own (plausibly abstracted from Florentine factional history, cf. Istorie fiorentine).

livy_content: famine, with two transmitted causes (bad year OR fields deserted for city politics; utrumque traditur)
machiavelli_content: Essendo la città di Roma aggravata dalla fame
notes: Event kept; Livy's double-tradition source criticism dropped (see aln:b-source-criticism).

livy_content: creation of L. Minucius as praefectus annonae — a new dedicated supply magistracy, corroborated by the libri lintei
notes: The institutional innovation at the heart of the crisis response is entirely absent from III.28. Machiavelli, who elsewhere celebrates Roman institutional creativity, drops a new magistracy.

livy_content: compulsory declaration of grain stocks; forced sale of surplus over one month's use; slave ration cuts; prosecution of dealers; inquisitorial audit; resulting suicides in the Tiber
machiavelli_content: non bastando le provisioni publiche a cessarla
notes: An entire scarcity-administration apparatus — the richest operational dataset in the pilot corpus — is compressed into five words: 'public provisions did not suffice'. The failure is kept; the machinery is deleted.

livy_content: Sp. Maelius ex equestri ordine, ut illis temporibus praedives
machiavelli_content: uno Spurio Melio, essendo assai ricco, secondo quegli tempi
notes: Near-verbatim echo including the relativizing clause ('rich for those times' — ut illis temporibus / secondo quegli tempi). Strong evidence of direct textual dependence; the equestrian order marker is dropped.

livy_content: grain bought in Etruria with private money through the agency of hospites and clientes; Livy conjectures this crowded out public procurement
machiavelli_content: fare provisione privatamente di frumento
notes: The procurement geography (Etruria), financing (privata pecunia), and the social network (guest-friends and clients) vanish into the adverb 'privatamente'. Livy's crowding-out conjecture — a genuine economic hypothesis — is also lost.

livy_content: grain largesses win the plebs; crowds escort him; clear hope of the consulship; then, appetite growing, plots regnum
machiavelli_content: pascerne col suo grado la plebe. Per la quale cosa, egli ebbe tanto concorso di popolo in suo favore
notes: Largesse → following preserved. But where Livy asserts an actual regnum conspiracy (weapons, bribed tribunes), Machiavelli keeps the danger prospective — see aln:b-threat-reframing.

livy_content: Livy: a real conspiracy is reported to the Senate (weapons stockpiled, assemblies at home, tribunes bought, kingship plans 'non dubia')
machiavelli_content: il Senato, pensando all’ inconveniente che di quella sua liberalità poteva nascere, per opprimerla avanti che la pigliasse più forze
notes: Decisive transformation: Livy's Senate reacts to intelligence of an armed plot; Machiavelli's Senate acts PREEMPTIVELY against the potential inherent in liberality itself. This converts a police action into a doctrine of preventive repression of private reputation — the chapter's thesis.

livy_content: Minucius learns of the plot because the same personnel circulate in both grain operations (in utraque domo genus idem hominum versaretur) and lays the evidence before the Senate
notes: The information-gathering mechanism — public and private administration sharing a workforce, creating an intelligence channel — is exactly the kind of administrative detail a chancery secretary might be expected to savor; it is dropped.

livy_content: the dictator is needed because consuls are bound by the appeal laws (constricti legibus de provocatione); a man 'freed from the chains of the laws' is required
machiavelli_content: per essere accecato il popolo da una spezie di falso bene, ordinò il Dittatore
notes: Livy's legal-constraint rationale (due-process protections make ordinary magistrates too slow) becomes an epistemic rationale (the people, blinded by false good, cannot be trusted to judge). Same institution, different theory of why it exists.

livy_content: named chain of command: consul T. Quinctius Capitolinus proposes; L. Quinctius Cincinnatus (aged 80+) dictator; C. Servilius Ahala master of horse
machiavelli_content: gli creò uno Dittatore addosso, e fecelo morire
notes: All names and the two-step command structure (dictator orders, master of horse executes) collapse into the office and the outcome. Note Machiavelli knows Ahala well — he appears in Disc I.5 — so the omission is compression, not ignorance.

livy_content: formal summons by apparitor; Maelius retreats into the crowd, appeals to the fides of the plebs; killed by Ahala while resisting
machiavelli_content: fecelo morire
notes: The legally crucial sequence (summons → refusal → killing justified by the refusal) is flattened to 'had him killed'. Machiavelli's version is MORE summary than Livy's legal record and closer to an execution.

livy_content: dictator's public legitimation: Maelium iure caesum... etiam si regni crimine insons fuerit, qui vocatus... non venisset — lawfully slain for refusing the summons even if innocent of the regnum charge
notes: The official legal theory of the killing is omitted; so is the precedent catalogue (Cassius, the decemvirs) and the bilibris farris sneer. Machiavelli needs the killing to be justified by the DANGER, not by a procedural refusal.

livy_content: goods sold by the quaestors into the treasury; house razed (Aequimelium); the confiscated grain distributed to the plebs at ONE AS PER MODIUS by Minucius, who receives a gilded-ox statue
notes: Omits the fiscal liquidation, the memorial sanction, the honorific economy, and the single hard price datum of the whole episode (1 as/modius). The state's repossession and re-pricing of the dangerous largesse — administratively the episode's punchline — is absent.

livy_content: tribunes agitate over the killing; election of military tribunes with consular power instead of consuls (only three, all patrician)
notes: The constitutional aftershock is dropped. In Machiavelli the dictatorial remedy is clean; in Livy it costs a round of institutional concession.

livy_content: Livy's documentary criticism: libri lintei cited for the prefecture; the tradition that Minucius became an 11th tribune rejected against a false statue inscription (refellit falsum imaginis titulum)
notes: Livy's handling of conflicting records — including his citation of physical documentary media (linen books, inscribed statue base) — is invisible in the Discorsi. Machiavelli's compression removes the evidentiary layer wholesale.

machiavelli_content: general theory: reputation through public ways (counsel, deeds) is safe and should be rewarded; through private ways (loans, dowries, protection from magistrates, food) breeds partisans and tyranny; Rome's triumphs, accuse and dictatorship mapped to this design
notes: The public/private reputation typology is Machiavelli's inference, not in Livy. The inventory of private favors (prestargli danari, maritargli le figliuole, difenderlo dai magistrati) is a recognizably Florentine patronage repertoire — plausibly chancery-era observational knowledge.

livy_content: a SERIES of distinct measures: Cassius's bill (486: conquered Hernican land + restitution of ager publicus; no holding cap), later tribunician bills, the Licinian-Sextian rogations (367: the iugera cap, Livy VI.35), the Gracchan laws (133, outside Livy I-X)
machiavelli_content: one continuous 'legge agraria' with two capi: a citizen holding cap in iugera, and division of conquered land
notes: The central compression of Case C: ~350 years of separate statutes fused into a single law with a stable two-clause content. The two capi are real but belong to different centuries (distribution: 486 onward; the cap: 367). This enables the 'one disease, one trajectory' narrative.

livy_content: Sp. Cassius: author of the first agrarian law; his Latin-inclusive allotment formula; the plebs' own rejection of his largesse as 'payment for kingship'; his execution with variant trial traditions
notes: Machiavelli names no author of the law in I.37 (Cassius does appear elsewhere, e.g. III.28's Livian precedent list he read). Omitting the founder-episode hides a datum awkward for I.37's class-conflict frame: the PLEBS killed the first agrarian proposer.

livy_content: tum primum lex agraria promulgata est, numquam deinde usaue ad hanc memoriam sine maximis motibus rerum agitata
machiavelli_content: mai non si parlò di questa legge in Roma, che quella città non andasse sottosopra
notes: Close echo of Livy's programmatic sentence — Machiavelli preserves exactly the generalization Livy himself flagged, down to the 'never... without upheaval' construction.

livy_content: scattered across Livy II-VI: consular armies led out, tribunes induced to veto colleagues, partial concessions, the Antium colony compromise (III.1)
machiavelli_content: systematic repertoire: o con trarre fuora uno esercito o che a quel Tribuno che la proponeva si opponesse un altro Tribuno, o talvolta cederne parte, ovvero mandare una colonia
notes: Machiavelli converts recurring narrative incidents into an explicit four-item tactical menu — a genuine analytic contribution: he extracts the elite's standard operating procedures from dispersed episodes.

livy_content: triumvirs appointed (T. Quinctius, A. Verginius, P. Furius); enrollment by name (nomina dare); so few enrolled that Volscian colonists filled the quota
machiavelli_content: con difficultà si trovò in Roma chi desse il nome per ire in detta colonia
notes: The enrollment datum is preserved and even flagged by Machiavelli as a 'termine notabile' of Livy — he notices the administrative record. But the commission's names and the Volscian back-fill (which falsifies 'the colony failed': it sailed, with non-Romans) are dropped.

livy_content: Livy's mechanism: abundance bred disdain (fecit statim, ut fit, fastidium copia) — satiety once land was actually offered
machiavelli_content: Machiavelli's mechanism: tanto era quella plebe più pronta a volere desiderare le cose in Roma, che a possederle in Anzio — preference for desiring near goods over possessing far ones
notes: Same datum, different psychology: Livy says supply killed demand; Machiavelli says distance killed demand (feeding his distance-decay account of the law's dormancy). A clean example of mechanism substitution on a preserved observation.

livy_content: — (Gracchi, Marius, Sulla, Caesar: all outside Livy I-X; Livy's own account survives only in periochae)
machiavelli_content: the law 'slept' until the Gracchi; reawakened, it destroyed liberty: plebs back Marius (four consulships, then three more), nobility backs Sulla; civil wars; Caesar heads Marius's party, Pompey Sulla's; Caesar wins and becomes Rome's first tyrant
notes: The entire late-republican trajectory is non-Livian (within this corpus): sources plausibly Plutarch (Gracchi, Marius, Sulla, Caesar lives), Sallust, Appian-tradition material, Florus/periochae. The 'quattro volte consule... tre altre volte' count for Marius matches Plutarch's seven consulships. This is the load-bearing evidence for 'the law destroyed the Republic' — and none of it is in the first decade.

livy_content: Livy marks the agrarian law as a perpetual source of upheaval, but assigns no republic-ending causal role within Books I-X
machiavelli_content: Da questo nacque il morbo che partorì la contenzione della legge agraria, che infine fu causa della distruzione della Republica
notes: The macro-causal thesis (agrarian contention → destruction of the Republic) is Machiavelli's construction, bridging Livian early material to non-Livian late material through a disease metaphor (morbo). It is argued, not sourced.

machiavelli_content: counterfactual defense of plebeian agitation: if agrarian contention took 300 years to enslave Rome, Rome would have reached servitude much sooner had the plebs not braked noble ambition with this law and other appetites
notes: Explicit counterfactual ('si sarebbe condotta, per avventura, molto più tosto in servitù') reconciling I.37 with I.4's tumults-produce-liberty thesis. No source; pure model-based reasoning.

machiavelli_content: normative premise: le republiche bene ordinate hanno a tenere ricco il publico e gli loro cittadini, poveri — well-ordered republics keep the treasury rich and citizens poor
notes: Stated as the standard against which the agrarian law is judged defective. Not in Livy II.41; resonates with Roman moralizing on paupertas Machiavelli knew (and with Disc III.25). Functions as an implicit fiscal-sociological design variable.
